extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literature; poets and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting criteria for assessing and composing poetry (especially classical, pastoral, and didactic forms). Emphasises subject-matter, originality, unity, voice, and the balance of invention/expression/inspiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essence of poetry: Invention, Expression, Inspiration
rubrics_metrics.description: "The essence of all poetry may be said to consist in three things, INVENTION, EXPRESSION, INSPIRATION."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a great inventive genius the other two elements (expression and inspiration) can scarcely be absent. But even without inventive power, a work may, by the power of expression alone or by the inspiration with which it is animated, fulfil the ends and be entitled to the name of poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predominance of feeling/inspiration leads to lyric quality
rubrics_metrics.description: "This feeling and inspiration form, indeed, a constituent part of all poetry; but in proportion as they come to be predominant qualities, the compositions in which they are embodied, approach nearer to the nature of lyrical poetry."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When inspiration/expression dominate over invention, the work tends toward lyricism. Use this balance to classify or judge a poem’s mode and intensity of feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of subject matter (avoid scientific/didactic misfits)
rubrics_metrics.description: "It requires no great acuteness to see, that scientific astronomy is a subject of this kind: and that a dissertation on some particular department of botany, or a series of medical lectures, although composed in verse, can never form a poem."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subjects incapable of poetical illustration (highly technical/scientific expositions) are inappropriate for poetry. Anti-pattern: forcing scientific material into verse produces false/artificial poetry (as in many Alexandrian learned poems). Exception historically when prose was unavailable and verse communicated knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Didactic/learned poetry is historically conditional and risky
rubrics_metrics.description: Learned (Alexandrian) didactic poetry belonged to a false and utterly artificial class of compositions; historically useful when prose was unpolished or unavailable to convey knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern poets should avoid imitating Alexandrian learned poetry because the original conditions (lack of prose, mythological personifications) no longer hold. Didactic verse may be justified only when its purpose is genuine transmission of knowledge and no better vehicle exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of mythology and personification as poetic material
rubrics_metrics.description: "The mythology of the Greeks... embraced the whole visible world within the circle of its bold personifications and delightful fables... placed within the proper province of ancient poetry."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mythology supplies rich, connective, and illustrative material for poetic invention. But modern poets must be cautious: many mythological inventions lack natural connection and can seem artificial when stitched together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and natural connection in narrative (avoid artificial interlacing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arranging many inventions or fables in consecutive order can only be accomplished by artificial omissions and unnatural interlacings, as in Ovid's Metamorphoses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid collecting disparate episodes or fables into a single work without organic links. Anti-patterns: anthology-like sequencing that forces continuity via artifice rather than natural relation; scoring negatively for lack of cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pastoral/bucolic should be integrated, not isolated
rubrics_metrics.description: The pastoral/Idyll should not be considered in an isolated manner, abstracted from its due situation in the general picture of the world and of human life which it is the province of poetry to unfold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pastoral scenes are more effective when set within larger social/human contexts (e.g., glimpses of rural life within heroic epics). Isolation leads to tautologies, repetitions, and unnatural exaggerations; integration yields truthful contrast and variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of voice in pastoral/Idylls
rubrics_metrics.description: Most Idylls betray their origin; shepherds and shepherdesses are often, in fact, gentlemen and ladies in disguise; even where true rustics appear, elegant language and wit can make us forget the rural scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain authentic, unsophisticated language and manners when representing rural speakers. Anti-pattern: refined wit and elegance that reveal courtly origin and break verisimilitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale and ambition: avoid diminutiveness and triviality
rubrics_metrics.description: "The exhaustion of her powers became daily more and more manifest, in the diminutiveness of all her productions. She soon gave birth to nothing, but little trifling buds and flowerets. Puns, conceits, and quibbles, were the fashion of the day."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discourage over-reliance on verbal cleverness, puns, conceits, and small artifices; prefer works of substantial imaginative scope and depth. Scoring should penalize trivial or purely ornamental effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality vs imitation: imitation must further native genius
rubrics_metrics.description: "Imitation alone is lifeless which aims not to extend the field, and increase the power of native genius, but merely to appropriate peculiar species of writing used by a foreign nation..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitation is acceptable only when it expands or enriches the imitator's native tradition; mere transplantation of foreign modes without creative extension is judged negatively. Preserve originality and adapt influences to national character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession of a single great, animating idea
rubrics_metrics.description: "The artist who excels... must be altogether animated and inspired with one great and indwelling idea... In like manner, every true poet, and every great inventive author, must be filled with some idea peculiarly his own... to which every thing else is subordinate."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a poet/author has a central unifying idea that shapes and gives coherence and power to their work. Works lacking a dominant conception risk superficiality; examples of excellence: Aeschylus, Pindar, Sophocles, Demosthenes, Herodotus, Thucydides, Aristotle, Plato.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve national individuality when borrowing
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is only necessary that we preserve our substantial individuality as a nation, that we do not part with the original peculiarities of our language and mode of thinking..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When borrowing forms or subjects from other cultures, maintain local language, modes of thought, and distinctive qualities. Anti-pattern: wholesale adoption that erases national character and produces a cold, unproductive transplant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learned/academic tone frequently produces obscurity
rubrics_metrics.description: Alexandrian academicians and librarians... as poets, they have all the defects into which learned poets are apt to fall; their mode of expression is rarely unaffected, and very often altogether obscure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of overlearned diction, excessive erudition, and obscure expression; prize clarity and unaffected expression. Scoring should penalize obscurity arising from pedantry rather than poetic density.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idylls as miniature pictures: strengths and pitfalls
rubrics_metrics.description: Idylls were 'little poetical pictures' sometimes mythological, often amatory; they can betray origin and become tautological or exaggerated when isolated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Idylls can succeed as focused, delicate portraits but must avoid repetitiveness, excessive refinement, and losing connection to broader human contexts. Positive scoring for vivid miniature effects; negative for self-contained banality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's purpose: to unfold human life and its connections
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry should not be abstracted from the general picture of the world and of human life, which it is the province of poetry to unfold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a poem illuminates human experience and situates particulars within wider human or worldly relations. Works that are insular, artificially confined, or irrelevant to human life should be judged as failing poetry’s chief purpose.
